Even after retirement, I stayed at home, managing the household and keeping the family’s traditions alive. I never had a driver’s license, and I have always relied on public transit or family members for transportation. My home, which I bought with a mortgage in 1965, has been my sanctuary for 58 years; the walls have seen my children grow up, the house has survived a few harsh winters, and the garden in the back has been a place of quiet reflection.

Living with a hearing impairment and a mental and emotional disability has shaped much of my daily routine. I use a cane or walker for short distances, and I have a transferable wheelchair for longer trips. My disability limits my daily travel—most of my outings are short, close to home, and often accompanied by my daughter or a friend. I don’t drive, so I have no vehicle available when using public transit, and I rarely, if ever, take the bus to work because I’m no longer employed.

I am the mother of the primary respondent in this survey. Watching my daughter grow into a woman and a mother herself has been my greatest pride. My days are filled with the quiet sounds of my garden, the occasional call from my grandchildren, and the soft music that I used to listen to on the radio. I am the father of my daughter, who is now a high‑school senior, and the grandfather of a 13‑year‑old son who is preparing for his freshman year. I still keep in touch with my daughter’s friends and my grandson’s teachers, often through phone calls or video chats, even though I’m both visually and hearing impaired. I use a cane for mobility and a walker for longer distances. Because of my disabilities, I’m unable to drive and I don’t have a driver’s license. Despite the challenges that my visual and hearing impairments present, I find joy in the simple moments: watching the sunrise from my porch, hearing my grandson’s laughter as he plays video games, and feeling the rhythm of my cane as I walk to the mailbox.
